summary: 9b continues the aggadic examination of Temple destruction. The bizayon kodashim (desecration of offerings) by Eli's sons is detailed (taking raw meat before the fat was burned), completing the Shiloh account from 9a. Then the First Temple's three cardinal sins are enumerated (avodah zarah, giluy arayot, shefichut damim), each independently proven from its own verse. The Second Temple's sin - sinat chinam (baseless hatred) - is declared equivalent to all three combined; the passage then notes that the First Temple generation, wicked as it was, still trusted in God, and traces the three decrees brought upon them to their three sins. A challenge follows - wasn't there sinat chinam in the First Temple too? - answered by R. Eliezer and scoped by a baraita to the nesi'im (leaders) specifically. R. Yochanan and R. Elazar then state the daf's structural principle: revealed sin gets a revealed end to exile, hidden sin does not - and R. Yochanan and Reish Lakish dispute, unresolved, which generation had greater merit. Finally, Reish Lakish's rebuke of Babylonian Jewry in the Jordan River (for not returning en masse with Ezra) is developed through Song of Songs' wall/door and silver/cedar imagery, with sasmagor and the bat kol explained, a critical question raised about the story's own transmission, and Rav Pappa's resolution - before the daf cuts off mid-thought on a further point about Ezra's generation and the Shechina, continuing on 10a.

display.title: Eli's sons: delayed bird-offerings and desecration of sacrifices
display.oneLine: The two sins of Eli's sons are detailed: delaying women's bird-offerings (treated by scripture as sexual immorality) and taking raw meat before the fat was burned (degradation of sacred offerings).
display.shortSummary: Eli's sons' delay of women's bird-offerings: although they did not commit adultery, their delay kept women at the Tabernacle and thus separated from their husbands - scripture holds them accountable as if they had cohabited with the women. Their second sin: bizayon kodashim. Before the fat of an offering was burned on the altar, a servant of the priests would come and demand raw meat for roasting. The man bringing the sacrifice would protest: 'Let them first burn the fat today, then take whatever you wish.' The servant would say: 'No, give it now or I will take it by force.' This brazen taking of raw, unburned meat was the desecration.
display.whats: This section closes the account of Shiloh's sins. Both sins are connected: the delay of bird-offerings kept women from purity and their husbands; the raw-meat taking showed contempt for the sacrificial order. Both involve the priests treating Temple service as an opportunity for personal benefit rather than divine service.
display.hint: The raw-meat verse says they took it 'before the fat was burned' - why does that specific sequencing make the taking a desecration rather than just a rude request?

learning.learnerQuestion: Why does scripture treat the delay of bird-offerings as equivalent to adultery?
learning.coreTension: The Talmud wants to be intellectually honest: Eli's sons were not adulterers. But the verse seems to say they were. The resolution: their sin had the effect that adultery would have had - women were kept from their husbands. Scripture 'credits' the transgressor with the downstream harm of his action.
learning.coreMove: This is a principle of scriptural attribution: when someone's action causes another person to commit (or be forced into a situation resembling) a sin, scripture attributes the original sin to the first person. The priests caused the women's extended absence from their husbands; scripture holds the priests responsible as if they had committed the act.
learning.resolution: The two sins of Shiloh are established: delayed bird-offerings (treated as giluy arayot) and taking raw meat prematurely (bizayon kodashim). Both involve priests prioritizing their own interests over proper Temple service.

takeaway.text: Scripture sometimes attributes a sin to a person based on the harm their action caused, even if they did not literally commit that sin. This principle - that indirect harm is treated as if direct - is used here to preserve Eli's sons from the charge of literal adultery while still holding them fully accountable.

reasoningPattern.notes: The Talmud regularly uses the principle that 'scripture ascribes the sin' to those who cause others to sin or suffer. Eli's sons caused women to remain impure and separated from their husbands - scripture treats this as their sin.

learning.ahaMoment: The raw-meat scene is vivid: a worshipper brings an animal, the priest's servant demands raw meat, the worshipper protests, the servant says 'give it now or I take it by force.' This is Temple service turned extortion - a shocking portrait of institutional corruption.
learning.learningBlocker: Students may think the 'delay of bird-offerings' means the priests refused to accept the offerings at all. In fact, they accepted them - but processed them slowly, keeping the women waiting for days.
learning.memoryAnchor: Two Eli-sons sins: delay the kanim (bird-offerings) - women stuck waiting, kept from husbands, scripture calls it immorality. Take raw meat before fat burned - intimidation and extortion of worshippers. Both: priests serving themselves, not God.

argumentFlow.label: Delayed bird-offerings kept women impure; scripture attributes the sin
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: Eli's sons delayed the processing of women's bird-offerings. Since the women had to wait, they could not achieve purity and could not return to their husbands. Scripture treats the priests as if they had committed the act of cohabitation themselves.

sourceRefs.note: Delayed bird-offerings attributed as giluy arayot

argumentFlow.label: Bizayon kodashim: raw meat seized before fat was burned
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: The desecration: a servant of the priests would demand raw meat before the fat was burned on the altar. The worshipper would protest. The servant would say: 'Give it now or I will take it by force.' This brazen seizing of raw meat - before the proper sacrificial sequence - was the bizayon kodashim.

sourceRefs.note: Bizayon kodashim scene detailed

visualizableElements.item: A worshipper bringing an animal to the altar; a priest's servant aggressively demanding raw, uncooked meat before the fat is burned; the worshipper protesting; the servant threatening force. Captures the extortion aspect of bizayon kodashim.
visualizableElements.label: Raw meat seizure scene

quizSeeds.question: Why does scripture treat the delay of women's bird-offerings as equivalent to sexual immorality?
quizSeeds.answer: Because the delay kept the women at the Tabernacle waiting, preventing them from achieving purity and returning to their husbands. Scripture attributes the downstream harm (forced separation from husbands) to the priests who caused it.

quizSeeds.question: What was the specific act of bizayon kodashim by Eli's sons?
quizSeeds.answer: Their servants would demand raw meat before the fat of the offering was burned on the altar. If the worshipper refused, they would take the meat by force. This violated the sacrificial order and treated sacred meat as personal property.

misconceptions.misconception: Eli's sons refused to accept women's bird-offerings entirely.
misconceptions.correction: They accepted the offerings but processed them slowly, causing women to wait extended periods - preventing them from achieving purity and returning to their husbands.

display.title: First Temple: three cardinal sins, each independently proven
display.oneLine: The First Temple was destroyed for avodah zarah, giluy arayot, and shefichut damim (three cardinal sins) - each independently proven from its own verse.
display.shortSummary: A Tosefta: the First Temple was destroyed for three things: avodah zarah (idolatry), giluy arayot (sexual immorality), and shefichut damim (bloodshed). Each is supported by a biblical verse. Idolatry: 'the bed is too short for both to lie' (Isaiah) - R. Yonatan reads this as the Sanctuary becoming too narrow once Manasseh's idol shared the space with God; R. Shmuel bar Nachmani says R. Yonatan wept when he reached this teaching. Sexual immorality: the daughters of Zion walked with outstretched necks, winking eyes, and mincing steps (Isaiah) - the Gemara expounds each phrase, and R. Yitzchak adds that they hid myrrh and balsam in their shoes to kick scent toward young men. Bloodshed: Manasseh filled Jerusalem with innocent blood from end to end (II Kings).
display.whats: This is the most famous passage in tractate Yoma, though its most famous line (sinat chinam equaling the three cardinal sins) belongs to the next sugya. Here, the Gemara grounds the First Temple's three-sin charge in independent verses rather than leaving it as assertion.
display.hint: The Tosefta charges the First Temple generation with three grave sins at once - how does the Gemara prove each one is really there in the text, rather than just asserting all three together?

learning.learnerQuestion: The Tosefta charges the First Temple generation with idolatry, sexual immorality, and bloodshed - what specific verse does it bring to prove each of these three sins?
learning.coreTension: A blanket charge of three grave sins is only as strong as its textual support. Each sin needs its own independent verse: how does the Gemara derive idolatry, sexual immorality, and bloodshed specifically from Scripture, rather than simply asserting all three together? And for sexual immorality specifically, does the Isaiah verse alone carry the charge, or does the Gemara need to expound it further?
learning.coreMove: For idolatry, R. Yonatan reads 'the bed is too short for both to stretch out' (Isaiah) as describing the Sanctuary itself: a space built for one that became too narrow once Manasseh's idol shared it with God - R. Shmuel bar Nachmani reports that R. Yonatan wept upon reaching this teaching. For sexual immorality, the Gemara expounds Isaiah's description of the daughters of Zion phrase by phrase (haughty gait, outstretched necks, painted eyes, mincing steps, tinkling anklets), and R. Yitzchak then adds a further detail: they hid myrrh and balsam in their shoes and kicked the scent toward young men of Israel to arouse them. For bloodshed, the Gemara cites the plain verse in II Kings: Manasseh filled Jerusalem with innocent blood from end to end. Each sin receives its own independent scriptural anchor.
learning.resolution: The three-sin charge is fully grounded: idolatry from the narrow-bed verse, sexual immorality from the daughters of Zion's catalogue (base exposition plus R. Yitzchak's addition), and bloodshed from the explicit verse about Manasseh filling Jerusalem with innocent blood. Each sin stands on its own textual foundation. The Gemara then turns to the Second Temple's own sin, taken up in the next sugya.

takeaway.text: The Tosefta's charge that the First Temple fell for idolatry, sexual immorality, and bloodshed is not left as assertion: each sin is independently proven from its own verse - the narrow bed for idolatry, the daughters of Zion's provocation for immorality, and Manasseh's innocent blood for bloodshed.

reasoningPattern.notes: A recurring exegetical move: when a Tosefta or baraita levels a multi-part charge, the Gemara does not let any single verse do double duty - each named sin gets matched to its own independent proof-text.

learning.ahaMoment: Each cardinal sin gets matched to its own verse rather than a single blanket citation: the 'narrow bed' image already describes the Sanctuary sharing space with an idol, and Isaiah's daughters-of-Zion catalogue - expounded phrase by phrase, then capped by R. Yitzchak's own added detail - describes the immorality, while Manasseh's own verse about filling Jerusalem with blood describes the bloodshed.
learning.learningBlocker: Students may treat R. Yitzchak's contribution as the Gemara's primary proof for giluy arayot. It is not - the Isaiah verse itself, expounded phrase by phrase, is the base proof; R. Yitzchak adds a further, more vivid detail (hidden perfume, kicked toward young men) on top of that base exposition, not in place of it.
learning.memoryAnchor: Three sins, three verses: a bed too narrow for two (idolatry), the daughters of Zion's provocative walk (immorality), Manasseh's innocent blood filling Jerusalem (bloodshed).

display.title: Second Temple destroyed for sinat chinam; First Temple generation trusted in God despite its sins
display.oneLine: The Second Temple generation studied Torah and practiced kindness, yet was destroyed for sinat chinam - declared equal to all three cardinal sins combined; the passage then notes that the First Temple generation, wicked as it was, still trusted in God, and traces the three decrees God brought upon them to their three sins.
display.shortSummary: The Second Temple generation engaged in Torah study, mitzvot, and acts of kindness. Why was the Temple destroyed? For sinat chinam (baseless hatred). This teaches that sinat chinam equals the three cardinal sins combined. The Gemara then returns to the First Temple generation: wicked as they were, they still trusted in God - proven by Micah 3:11, where even corrupt heads, priests, and prophets say 'is the Lord not among us? No evil shall befall us.' Therefore God brought upon them three decrees corresponding to their three sins, per Micah 3:12: Zion plowed as a field, Jerusalem in heaps, and the Temple Mount like the high places of a forest.
display.whats: This is the most famous passage in tractate Yoma. The sin of sinat chinam being equivalent to the three cardinal sins is not a claim about individual severity but about communal destruction capacity. The Temple requires a united people; sinat chinam makes unity impossible even among otherwise observant individuals. The passage then pivots back to the First Temple generation to make a further point: even in their wickedness, they retained trust in God, and their punishment (three decrees) is matched precisely to their three sins.
display.hint: How can a generation of Torah scholars and practitioners of kindness be destroyed for the same reason as a generation charged with idolatry, sexual immorality, and bloodshed?

learning.learnerQuestion: How can sinat chinam be equal to all three cardinal sins combined, and what does the passage then say about the First Temple generation's own trust in God?
learning.coreTension: The three cardinal sins (avodah zarah, giluy arayot, shefichut damim) are those for which a Jew must die rather than violate them. Sinat chinam is not in that category. So how does the Talmud equate them? The answer is structural: those sins destroy individuals or relationships with God. Sinat chinam destroys the entire social fabric. Separately, the passage raises a second point: even the wicked First Temple generation retained faith in God - so their punishment had to be measured precisely to their sins.
learning.coreMove: The comparison is communal destruction capacity, not individual severity. Pervasive sinat chinam prevents communal coherence, justice, and the social conditions that make Jewish life possible. Then, turning back to the First Temple: Micah 3:11 shows the corrupt leadership still declaring 'the Lord is among us, no evil shall befall us' - proof of retained trust despite wickedness - and Micah 3:12 shows God's three decrees matched precisely to their three sins.
learning.resolution: Sinat chinam's communal-destruction weight explains the Second Temple's fall. The First Temple generation's own sins are matched to three specific decrees (field, ruins, forest high-places), grounded in Micah 3:11-12. The Gemara next asks whether the First Temple was truly free of sinat chinam, taken up in the next sugya.

takeaway.text: Individual piety is not sufficient for communal survival. A generation of Torah scholars who hate each other cannot maintain a Temple. Separately, punishment can be precisely calibrated to sin, even for a generation that never lost its underlying trust in God.

reasoningPattern.notes: Sinat chinam is weighed by its effect on communal coherence, not by the individual-severity scale used for the three cardinal sins.

learning.ahaMoment: A generation of Torah scholars and practitioners of kindness falls for the same weight of sin as a generation charged with idolatry, immorality, and bloodshed - not because the sins are equally severe individually, but because sinat chinam destroys the very possibility of a functioning community.
learning.learningBlocker: Students may think the Second Temple generation was hypocritical - that they did not really practice Torah and mitzvot. The Talmud affirms they genuinely did; their failure was internal (hatred of each other), not external.
learning.memoryAnchor: Second Temple: Torah + mitzvot + kindness, yet destroyed for sinat chinam = weighed equal to all three cardinal sins. First Temple: wicked, yet still trusted in God (Micah 3:11) - so punished with three decrees matched precisely to their three sins (Micah 3:12).

No evil shall befall us.'

quizSeeds.question: How does the Talmud explain that the Second Temple generation - who studied Torah and performed kindness - was destroyed?
quizSeeds.answer: Because sinat chinam (baseless hatred) is considered equivalent in destructive power to all three cardinal sins combined. External piety without internal unity cannot sustain a Temple.

quizSeeds.question: What does Micah 3:11 prove about the First Temple generation, and what does Micah 3:12 explain?
quizSeeds.answer: Micah 3:11 shows that even the corrupt leadership retained trust in God ('is the Lord not among us?'). Micah 3:12 supplies the three decrees (field, ruins, forest high-places) that God brought upon them, matched to their three sins.

misconceptions.misconception: The Second Temple generation was hypocritical - they did not really practice Torah and mitzvot.
misconceptions.correction: The Talmud affirms they genuinely studied Torah, performed mitzvot, and practiced kindness. Their failure was not external behavior but internal: hatred of each other.

misconceptions.misconception: Sinat chinam is worse than murder or idolatry in terms of individual severity.
misconceptions.correction: The comparison is about communal destructive capacity, not individual severity. Sinat chinam destroys the social fabric of the entire community, making communal Jewish life impossible even among otherwise observant individuals.

display.title: First Temple sinat chinam: confined to the nesi'im
display.oneLine: A challenge - wasn't there sinat chinam in the First Temple too? - is answered: R. Eliezer identifies it as leaders who ate and drank together while slandering each other, and a baraita confirms it was confined to the nesi'im (leaders), not the general population.
display.shortSummary: But wait - was the First Temple free of sinat chinam entirely? A verse (Ezekiel: 'terrors of the sword are among my people; therefore strike your thigh') suggests otherwise. R. Eliezer explains: these are people who eat and drink with each other, yet stab each other with the swords of their tongues (slander). A baraita then confirms via the verse 'cry and wail, son of man, for it was against My people' that this applied specifically to the nesi'im (leaders and princes) of Israel, not the population generally.
display.whats: This section qualifies the sinat chinam argument: it was not entirely absent from the First Temple era. The key distinction (developed further in the next sugya) is scope: here, only the leadership harbored this hatred.
display.hint: If sinat chinam existed in the First Temple era too, why didn't it produce the same open-ended exile as the Second Temple's?

learning.learnerQuestion: If the First Temple generation had sinat chinam too, why didn't it prevent their exile from ending?
learning.coreTension: The sinat chinam argument seems to break down: both Temple eras had sinat chinam. The Gemara resolves this with a scope question: who exactly harbored the hatred?
learning.coreMove: R. Eliezer identifies the First Temple's sinat chinam concretely: people who ate and drank together while stabbing each other with slanderous words. A baraita then narrows the verse's target: it applied specifically to the nesi'im (leaders), not the general population.
learning.resolution: The First Temple's sinat chinam is confirmed but scoped: confined to the leadership. Whether and how this changes the exile-length picture is developed in the next sugya.

takeaway.text: A sweeping claim (sinat chinam destroyed only the Second Temple) survives a direct challenge by being scoped rather than abandoned: the First Temple did have sinat chinam, but confined to its leadership.

reasoningPattern.notes: A recurring Talmudic analysis: the same sin at different social levels has different consequences. Leadership-level sinat chinam is scoped differently than sinat chinam pervasive across an entire community.

learning.ahaMoment: R. Eliezer's image is vivid: people literally eating and drinking together while 'stabbing' each other with slander - sinat chinam does not require open conflict, only two-faced sociability.
learning.learningBlocker: Students may think this challenge fully undermines the earlier sinat-chinam argument. It does not - it refines it by scope (leadership vs. general population), a distinction the next sugya builds on.
learning.memoryAnchor: First Temple sinat chinam: real, but R. Eliezer locates it as leaders eating/drinking together while slandering each other, and a baraita confirms it was confined to the nesi'im, not the general population.

display.title: Revealed sin gets a revealed end; R. Yochanan and Reish Lakish dispute generational merit
display.oneLine: R. Yochanan and R. Elazar together teach that a generation whose sin is revealed gets a revealed end to its exile, while a generation whose sin is hidden does not; R. Yochanan then prefers the earlier generation, Reish Lakish argues for the later one, and R. Yochanan answers with the rebuilt Temple as proof.
display.shortSummary: Completing the baraita: the verse 'cry and wail, son of man' was specifically about the nesi'im of Israel. R. Yochanan and R. Elazar both taught: the earlier generations, whose sin was revealed, had their end [of exile] revealed; the later generations, whose sin was not revealed, did not have their end revealed. R. Yochanan then added his own preference: better the fingernails of the earlier generations than the belly of the later ones. Reish Lakish objected: on the contrary, the later generations are greater - even under the subjugation of foreign kingdoms, they engage in Torah study. R. Yochanan replied: let the Temple building prove it - it was restored to the earlier generation but not to the later one. His students then asked R. Elazar directly which generation was greater; he told them to look to the Temple building as their witness.
display.whats: This is where the Talmud actually states the principle that the earlier chapters of this sugya (9b's First and Second Temple material) have been building toward: revealed sin gets a revealed end to exile, hidden sin does not. The passage then pivots into a live dispute about generational merit that the Talmud does not resolve.
display.hint: Why would a generation whose sin was openly visible get a clearer end to its punishment than a generation whose sin stayed hidden?

learning.learnerQuestion: Why does a generation whose sin was revealed get a revealed end to its exile, while a generation whose sin was hidden does not?
learning.coreTension: The principle sounds backwards at first: shouldn't OPEN sin be worse, and hidden sin more forgivable? The Gemara's logic is functional, not moral: revealed sin can be named, rebuked by prophets, and therefore repented of on a knowable schedule. Hidden sin - like sinat chinam - cannot be identified or rebuked, so there is no mechanism by which its endpoint becomes knowable.
learning.coreMove: R. Yochanan and R. Elazar state the principle jointly. R. Yochanan then makes his own value judgment (earlier generations are preferable), which Reish Lakish directly challenges (later generations achieve more, given their harder circumstances). R. Yochanan's rebuttal appeals to an external, verifiable fact: the Temple was rebuilt for the earlier generation, not for the later one.
learning.resolution: The principle (revealed sin, revealed end) is established. The generational-merit dispute between R. Yochanan and Reish Lakish is not adjudicated here; R. Elazar, asked directly by his students, points them to the same Temple-building evidence R. Yochanan cited.

takeaway.text: A sin that can be named and rebuked carries within it the seeds of its own resolution; a sin that stays hidden has no such built-in endpoint. This is a claim about mechanism, not about which sin is worse.

reasoningPattern.notes: The structural principle underlying this whole daf's Temple-destruction discussion: an identifiable sin permits an identifiable resolution; an unidentifiable one does not.

learning.ahaMoment: R. Yochanan and Reish Lakish do not disagree about the historical facts - they disagree about how to weigh them. R. Yochanan sees the earlier generation's restored Temple as proof of greater merit; Reish Lakish sees the later generation's persistence in Torah study despite oppression as the greater achievement. The Talmud lets both stand.
learning.learningBlocker: Students may expect the Talmud to declare a winner between R. Yochanan and Reish Lakish. It does not - R. Elazar, asked the same question directly, answers with the same inconclusive appeal to the Temple building that R. Yochanan already used against Reish Lakish.

Elazar, asked directly: look to the Temple building.

quizSeeds.answer: A generation whose sin was revealed gets a revealed end to its exile (the First Temple's 70 years); a generation whose sin was hidden does not get a revealed end (the Second Temple's sinat chinam).

display.title: Reish Lakish rebukes Babylonian Jewry in the Jordan; sasmagor and bat kol explained
display.oneLine: Reish Lakish, swimming in the Jordan, denounces Babylonian Jewry for not returning en masse with Ezra, applying Song of Songs' wall/door and silver/cedar imagery; sasmagor and the bat kol are explained; the Gemara questions and resolves who was actually in the river, then cuts off mid-thought on a further point about Ezra's generation, continuing on 10a.
display.shortSummary: R. Elazar's answer completes: 'your witness is the Temple building.' Reish Lakish was swimming in the Jordan River; Rabbah bar bar Chana came and extended a hand to him. Reish Lakish said: 'I despise you [Babylonians]!' - quoting Song of Songs 8:9: 'if she is a wall, we will build upon her a turret of silver; if she is a door, we will enclose her with a cedar board.' Applied: had all Babylonian Jews ascended together with Ezra (like a wall), they would have been like silver, which rot cannot touch; since they ascended only partially (like a door), they are like cedar, which rot can reach. Ulla explains 'sasmagor' as the worm that hollows cedar from within; R. Abba says it alludes to the bat kol - once the last prophets (Chagai, Zechariah, Malachi) died, the Ruach HaKodesh departed from Israel, but the bat kol remained in use. The Gemara then questions whether Reish Lakish, famously selective about his associates, would really have spoken with Rabbah bar bar Chana; Rav Papa resolves it by proposing there was a third party - either Reish Lakish swam with Ze'iri extending the hand, or R. Elazar swam with Rabbah bar bar Chana extending the hand. When this reached R. Yochanan, he said that was not the reason. Alternatively [a further point]: had they all ascended in the days of Ezra, the Shechina would not have needed to dwell only partially in the Second Temple, as it is written 'may God enlarge Yefet, and let him dwell in the tents of Shem' - even... [the daf cuts off here, continuing to 10a].
display.whats: This closing passage on 9b ties together the cedar/sasmagor metaphor with the bat kol theme: both are statements about spiritual diminishment stemming from the incomplete return under Ezra. The daf ends mid-thought on a further point rather than with a tidy conclusion.
display.hint: By the time 9b ends, has the Gemara finished explaining its final point about Ezra's generation and the Shechina - or has it only just introduced it?

learning.learnerQuestion: Why is Reish Lakish so harsh toward Babylonian Jewry, and how far does the daf's final point about Ezra's generation actually get explained?
learning.coreTension: Reish Lakish's rebuke targets a historical failure (not returning en masse with Ezra), not the sage before him personally. The wall/door and silver/cedar imagery from Song of Songs is applied as precise allegory for complete vs. partial return and its effect on the Shechina.
learning.coreMove: Wall = unified complete return = silver (imperishable). Door = partial return = cedar (some solid, some rot). Ulla and R. Abba specify what that rot is: a literal worm (sasmagor), and allegorically the bat kol that replaced full prophecy. A critical aside then questions the story's own transmission (would Reish Lakish really speak with Rabbah bar bar Chana?), resolved by Rav Papa proposing alternate pairings - with the swimmer and hand-extender specifically swapped in the second option, not merely relabeled.
learning.resolution: Not fully reached within 9b. The Jordan story, its metaphor, and the transmission question are resolved; but the daf's final point - an alternative explanation involving Ezra's generation and the verse about Yefet dwelling in the tents of Shem - is only introduced before the daf cuts off mid-word, continuing on 10a.

takeaway.text: Historical rebuke in the Talmud can rest on precise, dual-layered imagery (a literal worm and an allegorical diminishment of prophecy) while the underlying story's own transmission is treated with critical scrutiny, not taken at face value.

reasoningPattern.notes: The same daf-boundary pattern seen elsewhere in this campaign: a final point is introduced but not completed, continuing to the next daf.

learning.ahaMoment: The Gemara does not just tell the Jordan story - it interrupts itself to ask whether the story's own cast of characters is even correct, given what is independently known about Reish Lakish's selectiveness in his associations. Rav Papa's resolution swaps BOTH who swam and who extended the hand between the two proposed pairings, not just the names.
learning.learningBlocker: Students may assume 9b ends with R. Yochanan's confirmation that the rebuke was justified. It does not: after R. Yochanan dismisses the transmission concern ('that is not the reason'), the Gemara raises a further, different point about Ezra's generation and the Shechina - and that point is cut off before it is explained, continuing on 10a.
learning.memoryAnchor: Wall+silver = complete return, full Shechina. Door+cedar = partial return, partial Shechina (sasmagor = literal worm and allegorical bat kol). Rav Papa: either Reish Lakish swam with Ze'iri extending the hand, or R. Elazar swam with Rabbah bar bar Chana extending the hand. Daf ends mid-thought on a further Ezra/ Shechina point, continuing to 10a.

quizSeeds.question: What is sasmagor, and what two things does the Gemara say it represents?
quizSeeds.answer: Literally, per Ulla, a worm that hollows cedar from within. R. Abba adds that it alludes to the bat kol - the diminished form of divine communication that remained after the last prophets died.

quizSeeds.question: What are Rav Papa's two possible pairings for who was in the Jordan, and does 9b end by confirming either one?

rashiTranslations.en: 'That they delayed their bird-offerings' - for the women would bring them at the completion of their days of childbirth, to be purified so as to eat consecrated food, and they were arrogant men and were lax in offering them, and the women

would wait there until they offered them, and so were delayed from returning to their place, to their husbands, and they thereby kept the women from procreation. 'Mehishtarea' - he expounds it as a notarikon,
'from ruling, one companion'. 'Two companions' - the image that Manasseh set up in the Sanctuary. 'Tzarah' is a term of rivalry, like two wives to one man, 'and her rival provoked her' (1 Samuel 1),

'and you shall not take a woman to her sister, to be a rival to her' (Leviticus 18). 'Its heads judge for a bribe' - the end of the verse is 'yet they lean upon the Lord, saying, is not the Lord in our midst' etc.
'And upon them' - it refers to the First Temple. 'And three'
'decrees' - 'a field', 'ruins', and 'high places of a forest'.
And 'iyin' means ruin, from 'with the broom of destruction' (Isaiah 14),
like 'and hail shall sweep away the refuge of lies' (ibid. 28).
'Whose sin was revealed' - they did not conceal
their transgressions. 'Their end was revealed' - 'when seventy years are completed
for Babylon I will remember you'
(Jeremiah 29). 'The latter, whose sin was not revealed'
- the people of the Second Temple were wicked
in secret. 'The Temple will prove it' - the Temple building.
'Set your eyes on the Temple' - the building of the Temple is a witness for you
in a matter that did not return to us but did return to the former ones.
'I hate you' - all the people of Babylon who did not go up
in the days of Ezra, and who thereby prevented the Divine Presence from coming
to rest again in the Second Temple. 'You would have been likened'
'to silver' - which does not rot; so too you would not have been
lacking the Divine Presence. 'Like doors' - a gate that has
two doors in it: one opens and its fellow
closes; so too you went up only in halves. 'That the rot'
'controls it' - part of it a worm eats
from within, and part of it remains; so too part of the vision of
the Divine Presence was there, but not all of it. 'What is'
'cedar' - what is this 'you were likened to a cedar' that he said? 'Ulla said:'
'sasmagor' - it crushes it and scrapes it
from within; sasmagor is the name of a worm. 'What is'
'sasmagor' - that is to say, why were they in the Second
Temple likened to sasmagor with regard to the resting of the Divine Presence?
'Rabbi Abba said: a bat kol' - there remained for them
just as there remains of the cedar a small part.
'Cast a man between them' - either the one bathing
changes, or the one who extended the hand: if it was Rabbi Shimon ben
Lakish who was bathing, Ze'iri extended him the hand;
or Rabba bar bar Chana extended him the hand
and Rabbi Elazar was the one bathing. 'When he came' - Rabbi Shimon
ben Lakish came before Rabbi Yochanan and recounted
to him: thus did I say to so-and-so.
'Even though' - the comment is completed on 10a.

glossary.en: Baseless hatred - hatred without cause. Identified by the Talmud as the sin that caused the destruction of the Second Temple and the longer exile.
Degradation of sacred offerings - a sin of Eli's sons who seized raw meat before the fat was burned on the altar, treating sacred service as an opportunity for personal benefit.
Heavenly voice - the diminished form of divine communication that replaced direct prophecy after the last prophets (Haggai, Zechariah, Malachi) died.
A wood-boring rot or insect that destroys cedar from within. Used metaphorically for the partial Shechina presence in the Second Temple due to incomplete aliyah.
